title: Hot flows in depth: SharedFlow, StateFlow and sharing
goal: By the end you can predict when a SharedFlow's emit waits, when tryEmit fails and which subscribers lose values under each overflow policy, say what a busy StateFlow collector will see, and pick a SharingStarted strategy from its exact start, stop and restart timeline.

warmup.q: A transition bus is `MutableSharedFlow<Int>(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = DROP_LATEST)`. A fast notifier and an audit writer that needs 1 s per row both subscribe. Six transitions are emitted 10 ms apart. What does the fast notifier receive?
options: All six: `DROP_LATEST` only drops values for the slow subscriber
1, 2 and 3: values 4, 5 and 6 are dropped for everyone
1 and 2: the buffer holds two values
warmup.why: Every subscriber reads from one shared buffer. The audit writer took 1 and is busy, so 2 and 3 fill the two slots it still needs. When 4 arrives the buffer is full, and `DROP_LATEST` throws 4 away before anyone can read it, notifier included. The same happens to 5 and 6.

sections.h: One slow subscriber decides what the fast one gets
sections.body:
A teammate wired up this transition bus. The notifier sends receipts and is fast. The audit writer needs a full second per row, so they picked `DROP_LATEST`: when the audit writer falls behind, it should drop transitions while the notifier carries on.

```kotlin
val bus = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST)
backgroundScope.launch { bus.collect { notifier += it } }              // fast
backgroundScope.launch { bus.collect { audit += it; delay(1_000) } }   // 1 s per row
for (transition in 1..6) { bus.emit(transition); delay(10) }
```

```java
// Java equivalent: a Reactor multicast sink; the audit subscriber requests one item, then stalls
Sinks.Many<Integer> bus = Sinks.many().multicast().directAllOrNothing();
bus.asFlux().subscribe(notifier::add);          // fast: unbounded demand
bus.asFlux().subscribe(auditThatRequestsOne);   // slow: request(1), then nothing
for (int t = 1; t <= 6; t++) bus.tryEmitNext(t);
```

Predict what the notifier receives. Here is the output in virtual time, with the other two policies for comparison:

```text
DROP_LATEST   notifier got [1, 2, 3]            audit got [1, 2, 3]
SUSPEND       notifier got [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]   audit got [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]   emit(4), (5), (6) returned at t=1000, 2000, 3000
DROP_OLDEST   notifier got [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]   audit got [1, 5, 6]
```

The notifier lost 4, 5 and 6, and it was never slow. To see why, picture a `MutableSharedFlow` as a radio station that records onto **one tape loop**. The emitter is the DJ, and every subscriber is a playback head on that same tape. There is no queue per subscriber. Old tape can only be cleared behind the slowest head, so the slowest subscriber decides when the tape is full, for everyone.

Walk through it. The audit writer takes 1 and starts its one-second write. Values 2 and 3 go onto the tape, which has room for exactly two (`extraBufferCapacity`). The notifier reads them at once, but that clears nothing, because the audit head still needs them. Value 4 finds the tape full, and the policy decides what happens:

- `SUSPEND`, the default: `emit(4)` waits until the audit writer takes 2, at t=1000. The notifier has nothing new to read, so it waits as well.
- `DROP_LATEST`: 4 is never recorded. Nobody hears it.
- `DROP_OLDEST`: 4 is recorded over 2, and the audit head is pushed past the part that was overwritten. Only the slow subscriber skips.

That makes the overflow policy a choice about every subscriber at once. When no transition may be lost and the notifier must not wait, keep `SUSPEND` and give the slow subscriber a buffer of its own. `bus.buffer(64).collect { ... }` puts a channel between the tape and the slow work (lesson 4 of this track), so the audit head takes values off the tape at once. In the Try it, that version delivers all six to both, and every `emit` returns by t=50. The cushion has a size: once those 64 slots fill, the audit side stops taking from the tape, and everyone waits again.

code.title: FastAndSlow.kt
code.src:
package workbench.flows.l07

import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi
import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.BufferOverflow
import kotlinx.coroutines.delay
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableSharedFlow
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.buffer
import kotlinx.coroutines.launch
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.advanceTimeBy
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runCurrent
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest

// One transition bus, two subscribers: a notifier that is fast, and an audit writer that
// needs 1,000 ms per row. Six transitions are emitted 10 ms apart.
// All times are virtual milliseconds (runTest), so the output is the same on every run.
@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
private fun busWith(policy: BufferOverflow, auditHasOwnBuffer: Boolean = false) = runTest {
    val bus = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = policy)
    val notifier = mutableListOf<Int>()
    val audit = mutableListOf<Int>()
    backgroundScope.launch { bus.collect { notifier += it } }
    val auditSide = if (auditHasOwnBuffer) bus.buffer(64) else bus   // a channel of its own in front of the slow work
    backgroundScope.launch { auditSide.collect { audit += it; delay(1_000) } }
    runCurrent() // both have subscribed and wait for a value

    val returned = mutableListOf<String>()
    for (transition in 1..6) {
        bus.emit(transition)
        returned += "$transition@t=$currentTime"
        delay(10)
    }
    advanceTimeBy(10_000); runCurrent()
    println(if (auditHasOwnBuffer) "$policy, audit collects bus.buffer(64)" else "$policy")
    println("  notifier got $notifier")
    println("  audit got    $audit")
    println("  emit returned: $returned")
}

fun main() {
    busWith(BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST)
    busWith(BufferOverflow.SUSPEND)
    busWith(BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)
    busWith(BufferOverflow.SUSPEND, auditHasOwnBuffer = true)
}

try.expect: `DROP_LATEST`: both get `[1, 2, 3]`, and every `emit` returns at once. `SUSPEND`: both get all six, but `emit(4)`, `emit(5)` and `emit(6)` return at t=1000, 2000 and 3000, so the fast notifier waits for the audit writer. `DROP_OLDEST`: the notifier gets all six and the audit writer `[1, 5, 6]`. With `bus.buffer(64)` on the audit side, both get all six and every `emit` returns by t=50. With a buffer of 3, `DROP_LATEST` gives both `[1, 2, 3, 4]`, and under `SUSPEND` the first to wait is `emit(5)`, which returns at t=1000. The Java twin shows the same choices with Reactor sinks: `directAllOrNothing()` refuses 2 to 6 for both subscribers (`FAIL_OVERFLOW`), a one-slot `onBackpressureBuffer` holds the notifier at `[1]` while the audit writer is stuck, `directBestEffort()` drops only for the stalled subscriber (a setting Kotlin's SharedFlow doesn't have), and `onBackpressureBuffer(64)` on the audit side frees the notifier.

sections.h: The exact rule: count what the slowest subscriber hasn't taken
sections.body:
`emit` is two steps in the source: `if (tryEmit(value)) return`, and only then suspend. So one rule answers both questions, when `emit` waits and when `tryEmit` returns `false`.

1. With no subscribers, every call succeeds. The value goes into the replay cache if `replay > 0`, and nowhere otherwise. `extraBufferCapacity` plays no part: with `replay = 2, extraBufferCapacity = 10`, five emits to nobody leave `replayCache = [4, 5]`.
2. With subscribers, the tape holds `replay + extraBufferCapacity` values, and it is full when the slowest subscriber has that many values it has not taken yet. Then `SUSPEND` makes `tryEmit` return `false` and `emit` wait, while the two drop policies return `true` and drop.

"Taken" has an exact meaning. A subscriber takes a value when it reads it off the tape, before your `collect` lambda runs. A value that a busy subscriber is still working on no longer counts. That is why the audit writer in the first section held only 2 and 3 against the tape, and not 1.

Now the default, `MutableSharedFlow()`, with no replay and no extra buffer. There is no tape at all, so a value can only pass like a **relay baton**. The runner (`emit`) holds it out and lets go once every receiver has a hand on it. `tryEmit` throws the baton without waiting, and it falls. `tryEmit` therefore returns `false` whenever there is a subscriber, even an idle one, as lesson 8 of the coroutines track said. And `emit` returns the moment the subscriber takes the value, before the subscriber has done anything with it: with 100 ms of work per value, `emit(1)`, `emit(2)` and `emit(3)` return at t=0, 100 and 200.

Here is the rule at work. One subscriber has subscribed and waits, then `tryEmit(1)` to `tryEmit(6)` run back to back (T is `true`, f is `false`):

| Flow | `tryEmit(1..6)` | The subscriber gets |
|---|---|---|
| `MutableSharedFlow()`, no subscriber | T T T T T T | (nobody there) |
| `MutableSharedFlow()` | f f f f f f | nothing |
| `extraBufferCapacity = 2` | T T f f f f | 1, 2 |
| `replay = 2` | T T f f f f | 1, 2 |
| `replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 2` | T T T f f f | 1, 2, 3 |
| `extraBufferCapacity = 2, DROP_OLDEST` | T T T T T T | 5, 6 |
| `extraBufferCapacity = 2, DROP_LATEST` | T T T T T T | 1, 2 |

Two rows deserve a second look. While someone is subscribed, `replay = 2` behaves exactly like `extraBufferCapacity = 2`: both are slots on the one tape. And three idle subscribers give the same row as one, because they share the tape.

The tape also explains a subscriber that arrives late. It is like walking into a cinema mid-film: you get the recap (the replay cache), then the live film. You never see the scenes the slow viewer in row 3 is still catching up on. With `replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 10`, a subscriber stuck on value 1 while 1 to 5 are emitted works through all five, and a second subscriber that joins after 5 gets only `[5]`.

Each `emit` returns at the same virtual time as `subscriber took`, so it waits for the take, not for the 100 ms of work. The late subscriber gets `[5]` while the first one works through `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`. In the Java twin the first `tryEmitNext` to an idle subscriber returns `OK` and the rest `FAIL_OVERFLOW`: a Reactor subscriber announces its demand with `request(1)` before anything is emitted, so the sink can hand one item straight over. With no subscriber Reactor answers `FAIL_ZERO_SUBSCRIBER`, where Kotlin answers `true` and the value goes nowhere. A `replay().limit(2)` sink accepts all six, and the stalled subscriber still gets all six once it asks: the limit only decides what a late subscriber gets, and the late subscriber to `limit(1)` gets `[5]`, as in Kotlin.

code.title: NoticeBoard.kt
code.src:
package workbench.flows.l07

import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers
import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi
import kotlinx.coroutines.delay
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableSharedFlow
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.update
import kotlinx.coroutines.launch
import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.UnconfinedTestDispatcher
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.advanceTimeBy
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runCurrent
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest
import java.math.BigDecimal
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger

data class Quote(val pair: String, val mid: BigDecimal)

// A StateFlow is a notice board with one slot. Parts A, B, C and E use virtual time.
@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() {
    runTest {
        println("== A: equal values")
        val first = Quote("EURUSD", BigDecimal("1.0850"))
        val board = MutableStateFlow(first)
        val seen = mutableListOf<Quote>()
        backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { board.collect { seen += it } }
        board.value = Quote("EURUSD", BigDecimal("1.0850"))   // equal fields
        println("  after an equal set: board still holds the first object? ${board.value === first}")
        board.value = Quote("EURUSD", BigDecimal("1.08500"))  // one more zero
        println("  collector saw ${seen.map { it.mid }}")
    }
    runTest {
        println("== B: AUTHORIZED -> CAPTURED -> AUTHORIZED while the collector is busy")
        val status = MutableStateFlow("AUTHORIZED")
        val log = mutableListOf<String>()
        backgroundScope.launch { status.collect { log += "t=$currentTime $it"; delay(100) } }
        runCurrent()
        delay(10); status.value = "CAPTURED"
        delay(10); status.value = "AUTHORIZED"
        advanceTimeBy(500); runCurrent()
        println("  busy collector saw $log")
    }
    println("== C: compareAndSet")
    val count = MutableStateFlow(10)
    println("  cas(10, 11) = ${count.compareAndSet(10, 11)}, value ${count.value}")
    println("  cas(10, 12) = ${count.compareAndSet(10, 12)}, value ${count.value}  (stale expect)")
    println("  cas(11, 11) = ${count.compareAndSet(11, 11)}, value ${count.value}  (true, and nobody is woken)")

    println("== D: update { } from 8 coroutines x 100,000 on Dispatchers.Default (REAL threads)")
    val calls = AtomicInteger()
    val counter = MutableStateFlow(0)
    runBlocking(Dispatchers.Default) {
        repeat(8) { launch { repeat(100_000) { counter.update { calls.incrementAndGet(); it + 1 } } } }
    }
    println("  value=${counter.value}, the lambda ran ${calls.get()} times")

    runTest {
        println("== E: subscriptionCount keeps every change")
        val events = MutableSharedFlow<Int>()
        val counts = mutableListOf<Int>()
        backgroundScope.launch { events.subscriptionCount.collect { counts += it } }
        runCurrent()
        val visitor = backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { events.collect { } }
        visitor.cancel() // joined and left before the observer ran again
        runCurrent()
        val plain = MutableStateFlow(0); val plainSeen = mutableListOf<Int>()
        backgroundScope.launch { plain.collect { plainSeen += it } }
        runCurrent()
        plain.value = 1; plain.value = 0; runCurrent()
        println("  subscriptionCount observer saw $counts; a plain StateFlow doing 0 -> 1 -> 0 showed $plainSeen")
    }
}

try.expect: A: the board still holds the first object after the equal set, and the collector sees `[1.0850, 1.08500]`. B: only `[t=0 AUTHORIZED]`. C: `true`, `false`, `true`, with the value still 11. D: exactly 800000, with the lambda run far more than 800,000 times (1,405,098 in one run here). E: `[0, 1, 0]` against `[0]`. In the Java twin, `BigDecimal.equals` says 1.0850 and 1.08500 differ while `compareTo` says they are equal. The plain replay sink delivers all three statuses, and the one with `onBackpressureLatest().distinctUntilChanged()` delivers only `[AUTHORIZED]`. `AtomicReference.compareAndSet` fails because it compares references, and the expected `BigDecimal` is a different object. `updateAndGet` re-runs its lambda the same way. `currentSubscriberCount()` is a plain number, 0 before and after the visitor, with no record of the visit.

sections.h: Sharing is one pump and many taps
sections.body:
`stateIn` and `shareIn` read like conversions, and each one launches a coroutine. `shareIn(scope, started, replay)` creates a `MutableSharedFlow` with that `replay`, an extra buffer that brings it up to at least 64 slots, and `SUSPEND`. Then it launches one coroutine in `scope` that collects the upstream into it. `stateIn` does the same with a `MutableStateFlow(initialValue)`. Picture a building with one water pump (that coroutine) and a tap for every subscriber. `started` decides when the pump runs. `Eagerly` runs it from opening time, whether anyone is there. `Lazily` lets the first visitor switch it on, and nobody ever switches it off. `WhileSubscribed(5_000)` is a tap on a motion sensor that shuts the water off 5 s after the last person leaves.

Inside, `WhileSubscribed` watches `subscriptionCount`. When the count drops to 0, it waits `stopTimeout` and then sends STOP, which cancels the upstream collection. A subscriber who comes back first cancels that pending wait, so the pump never stopped. The figure shows an exact virtual-time run for an FX poller that emits `run * 100 + i` every second. Dashboard A leaves at 2.5 s and is back at 4 s: it gets 104, from the same run. A leaves again at 6 s, and STOP comes at 11 s. When A returns at 14 s, it gets the stale 111 first, and then 200 from run #2.

Three facts in that run catch people:

- The upstream restarts from the top, because it is a cold flow collected again. Run #2 counts from 200, and a `runningFold` would start over.
- The returning subscriber sees the stale value first. `replayExpirationMillis = 0` resets the StateFlow to its initial value when the pump stops, so the late A gets -1 instead of 111.
- With `WhileSubscribed()`, whose stop timeout is 0, every page reload is a STOP and a new START.

```kotlin
val live: StateFlow<Rate?> = feed.stateIn(
    appScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000, replayExpirationMillis = 0), initialValue = null)
```

```java
// Java equivalent: connect with the first subscriber, disconnect 5 s after the last.
// After a disconnect Reactor reconnects with an empty replay cache, so no stale rate is shown.
Flux<Rate> live = feed.replay(1).refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5));
```

Reading `.value` is not a subscription. It is looking at the tap from the doorway, and it doesn't trip the sensor. A request cache built with `Lazily` or `WhileSubscribed` and read only through `.value` never starts: in the Try it, three requests at 3.5 s read `[null, null, null]`, and the feed was fetched 0 times. With `Eagerly` they read the latest rate after 4 fetches.

Two more ways the pump goes wrong. If the upstream throws, the sharing coroutine dies and the exception goes to the scope's handler. Subscribers are not told. They stand at their taps and wait for ever, so put `retry` or `retryWhen` above `shareIn`. And `shareIn` inside a function that each request calls installs a new pump per call: 50 requests that each read one value left 50 sharing coroutines and 500 upstream polls after 10 s. Build the shared flow once, in a field, in a scope that you cancel when the service stops.

try.expect: The default run: START #1 at 0, A gets 104 at 4000 with no restart, STOP #1 at 11000, and at 14000 A gets 111, then START #2 and 200, for 2 starts in all. In the `.value` part, `WhileSubscribed` and `Lazily` read `[null, null, null]` with 0 fetches, and `Eagerly` reads `[1.0854, 1.0854, 1.0854]` after 4 fetches. With `expire`, A gets -1 instead of 111 at 14000. With `stop0`, STOP #1 comes at 2500 and START #2 at 4000, where A gets the stale 102 and then 200; STOP #2 at 6000 and START #3 at 14000 make three starts. The Java twin keeps run #1 through the first return (A gets 104), stops about 500 ms after A leaves the second time, and on the late return prints START #2 and then 200 with no stale value, because Reactor's `replay(1)` begins a fresh cache for the new connection. Its times vary by a few ms.

analogy: A cold flow is a recording: everyone who presses play hears it from the start, on their own player. A hot flow is a radio station: one broadcast, and you hear whatever is on air when you tune in. A `SharedFlow` station records onto one tape loop that every listener's playback head reads, so the slowest listener decides when the tape is full. A `StateFlow` is a notice board with one sheet, and readers only look up when they have a moment. `stateIn` and `shareIn` are the building's water pump: `Eagerly` runs it from opening time, `Lazily` is switched on by the first visitor and never off, and `WhileSubscribed` is a motion sensor with a delay. The analogy breaks at the tape. A real radio station never waits for its slowest listener, and a SharedFlow with `SUSPEND` does exactly that.
in_your_world: In a payment service the hot shapes map onto different jobs. The FX rates that request handlers read through `.value` are a cache: `stateIn(appScope, Eagerly, null)` with a retry above it, as in the lab, because a cache that waits for a subscriber never fills. The live rates pushed to ops dashboards over server-sent events are a tap: `WhileSubscribed(5_000, replayExpirationMillis = 0)`, so a page reload keeps the provider connection and a dashboard opened at night never shows an old rate. Payment transitions that a notifier and an audit writer both consume are events: a `MutableSharedFlow` with a buffer, `SUSPEND`, a checked `tryEmit` from the Kafka listener thread, and a buffer of its own in front of the slow audit writer. And when a fraud handler and a ledger handler share one poll loop, the tape keeps nothing for a handler that subscribes late (with `replay = 0`): the records polled before it arrived are gone for it, unless the sharing waits for both, as in the worked example.
mistake: The most common mistake is a request cache copied from dashboard code: `rates.stateIn(appScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null)`, read in every handler with `.value`. Nothing ever collects it, and reading `.value` is not a subscription, so the feed never starts and every handler gets `null`. `Lazily` has the same trap. It passes a unit test that collects the flow to check it, which is the one thing the production code never does. Pick the strategy by who reads. Code that only reads `.value` needs `Eagerly`, or the suspend `stateIn(scope)` at start-up. Code that collects can use `WhileSubscribed`. Then put `retry` above `stateIn`, or the first feed error stops the cache for good while it keeps serving its last rate.

compare.title: One FX feed, shared for request handlers and for dashboards

java.title: FxRates.java (Reactor)

kotlin.title: FxRates.kt (StateFlow)

compare.note: The Kotlin side needs no `AtomicReference`, because a StateFlow is both the holder and the stream: `.value` reads it synchronously, and collectors get the same value with equality conflation built in. Lifetime differs too. Both Kotlin flows live in `scope`, so cancelling that one scope stops both upstream collections; in Reactor the cache lives as long as its `Disposable`, and the dashboard connection as long as it has subscribers. The two sides also forget differently. After a disconnect, `replay(1).refCount` reconnects with an empty cache, and Kotlin needs `replayExpirationMillis = 0` for the same effect. Errors are where they differ most. In Reactor an error in the feed reaches every subscriber as `onError`. In Kotlin it ends the sharing coroutine, goes to the scope, and leaves the subscribers waiting, which is why the `retry` sits above `stateIn`. Both versions open two connections to the provider, one per view.

worked.title: Share one poll loop between a fraud handler and a ledger handler

steps.say: A service polls a Kafka-style source and hands every record to two handlers, fraud checks and ledger posting. Polling twice would read every record twice, so the poll loop is shared with `shareIn` and `replay = 0`. As their beans start, the fraud handler subscribes at 250 ms and the ledger handler at 500 ms. Predict what each has received by 800 ms.
steps.code:
var offset = 0
val records = flow { while (true) { delay(100); emit("rec-${offset++}") } }   // stands in for poll()
val shared = records.shareIn(appScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly)                 // replay = 0
// fraud subscribes at t=250, ledger at t=500

steps.say: The virtual-time run. With `Eagerly`, `rec-0` and `rec-1` were polled before anyone listened, and the ledger handler also missed everything up to `rec-4`. `WhileSubscribed()` helps the first handler and not the second. With `replay = 0` the tape keeps nothing for a late subscriber.
steps.code:
Eagerly:            fraud=[rec-2, rec-3, rec-4, rec-5, rec-6]  ledger=[rec-5, rec-6]
WhileSubscribed():  fraud=[rec-0, rec-1, rec-2, rec-3, rec-4]  ledger=[rec-2, rec-3, rec-4]

steps.say: Start the poll only when both handlers are there. `SharingStarted` is a `fun interface` that turns the subscriber count into START and STOP commands, so the gate is one line. In the same run, both handlers now get `[rec-0, rec-1]` by 800 ms.
steps.alt_code:
// 1. and 2.: connect once two subscribers are there (Reactor's version never disconnects)
Flux<String> shared = records.publish().autoConnect(2);

steps.say: Self-check: the ledger handler needs 50 ms per record and fraud needs 5 ms. With `shareIn`'s default `SUSPEND`, which one sets the pace of the poll loop, and is that what you want here? (The ledger handler. The tape is full once the slowest handler has 64 records it hasn't taken, and then `emit`, the poll loop, waits. For records that must all be processed, that is the backpressure you want. A drop policy would lose records with no error.)

lab.title: Predict the tape, then share an FX feed two ways
steps: Run the tests. 24 of 25 fail: every `SharedFlowRuleTest` case and five of the six `FxRatesTest` cases.

In `SharedFlowRule.kt`, write `predictTryEmits` from the rule in the second section, without creating a flow. For each row, the test runs a real `MutableSharedFlow` and compares. Then write `predictReceived`.

In `FxRates.kt`, fix `requestCache`. Handlers only read `.value`, so pick the `SharingStarted` that doesn't wait for a subscriber, and add a retry above `stateIn` that waits 1,000 ms after an `IOException`.
Fix `dashboardFeed`: survive a reload within 5 s, stop 5 s after the last dashboard leaves, and reset to `null` when it stops.
Run the tests until all 25 pass. Then read how `FxRatesTest` counts feed starts and stops in virtual time, and why it never calls `advanceUntilIdle()`.
hints: The rule has three cases: no subscribers, a drop policy, and `SUSPEND`. In the last one the answer depends only on the index of the call and `replay + extraBufferCapacity`.
`predictReceived`: `SUSPEND` and `DROP_LATEST` keep the first values that fit, and `DROP_OLDEST` keeps the last ones.
`retry { e -> ... }` takes a suspending predicate, so it can `delay(1_000)` before it returns `true`. It must sit before `stateIn`: once the sharing coroutine has died, nothing restarts it.
If the late-dashboard test sees the old rate first, you need the second parameter of `WhileSubscribed`.

drill.title: A transition bus, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `class TransitionBus` with `fun publish(t: Transition): Boolean`, called from a non-suspending Kafka listener callback, and `val events: SharedFlow<Transition>`. A burst of up to 64 transitions must not be refused, no transition may be dropped by a policy, and a slow audit subscriber must not hold back a fast notifier. Write the audit subscriber's collection too, and say in a comment when `publish` returns `false`.

alt.title: Java equivalent

recap: A `MutableSharedFlow` is one buffer of `replay + extraBufferCapacity` slots shared by every subscriber. It is full when the slowest subscriber has that many values it hasn't taken, and a subscriber takes a value before its `collect` lambda runs.

When it is full, `SUSPEND` makes `emit` wait and `tryEmit` return `false`, `DROP_LATEST` drops the new value for everyone, and `DROP_OLDEST` makes only the slow subscriber skip. With no subscribers nothing ever waits.

The default `MutableSharedFlow()` has no buffer: a value passes like a relay baton, so `tryEmit` fails whenever anyone is subscribed, and `emit` returns once every subscriber has taken the value. A late subscriber gets the replay cache, then live values.

A StateFlow compares with `equals` when you set it and again in each collector. A busy collector sees only the latest value, so A, B, A while it is busy shows nothing. `update { }` may run its lambda many times.

`shareIn` and `stateIn` launch one coroutine in your scope. `WhileSubscribed(5_000)` survives a return within 5 s; after a stop the upstream restarts from the top, behind the stale value unless `replayExpirationMillis = 0`.

Reading `.value` is not a subscription, an upstream failure leaves subscribers waiting, and `shareIn` per call leaks a coroutine per call. Use `Eagerly` for caches, `retry` above the share, and one shared flow per service.

quiz.q: Three subscribers have subscribed to `MutableSharedFlow<Int>(replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 2)` and are waiting. Code calls `tryEmit(1)` to `tryEmit(5)` back to back, so no subscriber runs in between. What do the five calls return?
options: true five times: replay keeps values, so the flow never refuses one
true, true, false, false, false: only `extraBufferCapacity` counts
true five times: each subscriber has its own three slots, nine in all
quiz.why: The buffer has `replay + extraBufferCapacity` = 3 slots, and all three subscribers share them. None of them can take a value between the calls, so the fourth call finds the slowest subscriber with 3 untaken values, and `SUSPEND` refuses it. While anyone is subscribed, replay slots are ordinary buffer slots, and there is no queue per subscriber.

quiz.q: A payment's `StateFlow<Status>` goes CAPTURED, then REFUND_PENDING, then CAPTURED again within 5 ms, while its only collector is inside a 50 ms database write that started after it got CAPTURED. What does the collector get when the write finishes?
options: Nothing new: the current value equals the last one it got
quiz.why: A waking collector reads the one slot and emits only if the value differs from the one it emitted last. The slot holds CAPTURED, equal to what it last saw, so nothing is emitted. If every transition matters, the stream should be a SharedFlow with a buffer.

quiz.q: An SSE endpoint shares an FX feed with ops dashboards. A page reload must not reconnect to the provider, and a dashboard opened after the feed has stopped must never show the old rate. Which `started` fits `stateIn(scope, started, null)`?
quiz.why: The 5 s stop timeout covers the reload: a subscriber that comes back cancels the pending stop. The second parameter resets the StateFlow to `null` when the feed stops, so a later dashboard sees `null`, then a fresh rate. Plain `WhileSubscribed(5_000)` shows the stale rate first, and `Eagerly` and `Lazily` never stop at all.

quiz.q: `prices.shareIn(appScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, replay = 1)` has two subscribers. The upstream sends two prices, then throws `IOException("feed reset")`. What happens next?
options: The sharing coroutine fails, the scope's handler gets the exception, and the subscribers keep waiting with no error
`shareIn` restarts the upstream on its own
quiz.why: The upstream runs in the sharing coroutine, not in the subscribers. Its exception ends that coroutine and goes to the scope, and the subscribers are never told: in the measured run the subscriber had `[1, 2]` and was still waiting a second later. Put `retry` or `retryWhen` above `shareIn`.

quiz.q: From lesson 4 of this track: `postings.buffer(10).collect { ... }`, and the collector is stuck on its first posting. How many of the producer's `emit` calls have returned?
quiz.why: Ten postings wait in the buffer and one is in the collector's hands, so 11 calls returned and the 12th is suspended. `shareIn` follows the same arithmetic: with its default 64-slot buffer, the upstream ran 65 emits ahead of a stuck subscriber.

flashcards.front: Default `MutableSharedFlow()` with one idle subscriber: what does `tryEmit` return?
flashcards.back: `false`. There is no buffer, so a value can only pass from a suspended `emit` to a subscriber taking it (a rendezvous). With no subscriber at all it returns `true` and the value goes nowhere.

flashcards.front: When is a MutableSharedFlow's buffer full?
flashcards.back: When the slowest subscriber has `replay + extraBufferCapacity` values it hasn't taken yet. With no subscribers it is never full.

flashcards.front: One subscriber stalls under `DROP_LATEST`. Does the fast subscriber lose values too?
flashcards.back: Yes. The dropped value was never stored, so nobody gets it. Only `DROP_OLDEST` limits the skipping to the slow subscriber.

flashcards.front: What does a subscriber that joins a SharedFlow late receive?
flashcards.back: The replay cache, then live values. Never the backlog that slower subscribers are still working through.

flashcards.front: A StateFlow goes A, then B, then A while its collector is busy. What does the collector see when it is free?
flashcards.back: Nothing new. It reads the current value (A), which equals the last one it emitted, so it emits nothing.

flashcards.front: Does reading `stateFlow.value` start a `Lazily` or `WhileSubscribed` upstream?
flashcards.back: No. `.value` is not a subscription. A cache that is only read through `.value` needs `Eagerly` (or the suspend `stateIn(scope)`).

flashcards.front: `WhileSubscribed(5_000)`: the last subscriber leaves and a new one arrives 2 s later. Does the upstream restart?
flashcards.back: No: the pending stop is cancelled and the same run continues. After more than 5 s it restarts from the top, and the newcomer first sees the stale value unless `replayExpirationMillis = 0`.

terms.plain: A flow that runs whether or not anyone collects it, and shares what it produces with whoever is subscribed. SharedFlow and StateFlow are hot.
The one array of `replay + extraBufferCapacity` slots that every subscriber of a MutableSharedFlow reads from, each at its own position. There is no queue per subscriber.
A hand-over with no buffer: the value passes only while the sender waits and the receiver takes it. The default `MutableSharedFlow()` works this way.
The moment a subscriber reads a value off the shared buffer, before its `collect` lambda runs. Only values not yet taken count against the buffer.
StateFlow ignores a set that equals the current value, and a waking collector skips a value equal to the last one it emitted.
The one coroutine that `shareIn` or `stateIn` launches in your scope to collect the upstream. It lives as long as the scope, whatever the subscribers do.
How long `WhileSubscribed` waits after the last subscriber leaves before it cancels the upstream. A subscriber who returns sooner cancels the stop.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks two things: why did the fast notifier lose transitions under `DROP_LATEST` when only the audit writer was slow, and why does `tryEmit` on a default `MutableSharedFlow()` fail while the subscriber is idle? Answer both with the tape model, in a few sentences.
explain_back.answer: A MutableSharedFlow keeps one buffer of replay + extraBufferCapacity values, and every subscriber reads it at its own position. A value can only be cleared once the slowest subscriber has taken it, so the slowest subscriber decides when the buffer is full, for everyone. Under DROP_LATEST a value that finds the buffer full is never stored, so the fast notifier never sees it either. The default flow has no buffer at all. A value can only pass from an emit that is suspended and waiting to a subscriber that takes it, like a relay baton. tryEmit can't wait, so with any subscriber present it returns false, idle or not. With no subscriber it returns true, and the value goes nowhere.

deeper.body:
The internals, for a curious day. The field names here are private and may change in any release, so don't build on them.

Every collector of a shared flow gets a slot object from an array that starts at size 2 and doubles when full: 2 for one or two subscribers, 4 for three or four, 8 for five. A SharedFlow slot holds the index of the next value its collector will read, plus that collector's suspended continuation. The tape is a ring buffer, also allocated lazily and doubled when needed, and it holds the buffered values followed by the suspended `emit` calls as placeholder objects. Its start, `head`, is the smaller of the slowest collector's index and the start of the replay cache. When the slowest collector moves on, `head` moves, the old cells are cleared, and waiting emitters are resumed as their values move onto the tape. Every change happens under one lock, and the coroutines to resume are collected and resumed after the lock is released. The KDoc puts the cost of an emit at O(N) in the number of subscribers.

A StateFlow slot is one atomic field: free, waiting, pending, or a suspended continuation. An update marks every slot pending and copies nothing, which is why the KDoc calls StateFlow allocation-free. Concurrent updates use a sequence number that is odd while an update is being delivered. A second writer that arrives in the middle only bumps it, and the first writer loops round to deliver the newest value.

Two APIs in this area are experimental in 1.11.0 and need `@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)`. `resetReplayCache()` empties the replay cache for new subscribers, while existing ones keep what they had; on a `MutableStateFlow` it throws `UnsupportedOperationException: MutableStateFlow.resetReplayCache is not supported`. `SharedFlow.asFlow()`, new in 1.11.0, hides the hot type from callers.

The suspend overload `stateIn(scope)` has no `started`. It launches the upstream in `scope`, suspends until the first value, and returns a StateFlow holding it: in one run, a config flow whose first value took 300 ms made `stateIn` return at t=300. That fits a config value loaded at start-up. An empty upstream throws `NoSuchElementException: Flow is empty`. An upstream that fails before its first value rethrows to the caller and also cancels the scope you passed, so choose that scope knowing it goes down with a failed load.
